title: DLF has Rs 75,000 crore of homes it cannot count as revenue yet
subtitle: DLF sold plenty of homes, yet its revenue fell. Here is why a builder's bookings and revenue are different, and why it expects growth from FY28.
content_html:
Picture this. A company has sold homes worth tens of thousands of crores of rupees, yet its revenue for the latest three months went down. That is the puzzle at DLF, India's largest listed real estate company. On Saturday, 17 October 2026, its finance chief told analysts that launched projects worth around Rs 75,000 crore are nearing completion, and that revenue growth should speed up from FY28.

So where is all that money hiding? The answer is a simple rule about when a builder is allowed to count a sale.

What happened this week?

On Friday, 16 October, DLF shared its results for July to September 2026. Its net profit, the money left after all costs and taxes, rose 10 per cent to Rs 1,301.35 crore. But its revenue from operations, the money earned from its main work, fell 23 per cent to Rs 1,261 crore, down from Rs 1,643 crore a year earlier.

How can profit go up while revenue goes down? Part of the answer is "other income", money that does not come from selling homes, such as interest. DLF's other income was Rs 881 crore, up from Rs 460 crore a year before.

The next day, on the call with analysts, the company explained why its revenue looks small today and why it expects that to change.

Bookings and revenue are not the same thing

Think of a tailor before the wedding season. A customer orders a sherwani today and pays an advance. The order is real. But the tailor has not finished the job yet. Only when the sherwani is stitched and handed over is the work truly done.

Builders work the same way. A "sales booking" (also called pre-sales) is when a buyer signs up for a flat and starts paying. In July to September, DLF booked homes worth Rs 3,800 crore. It also collected Rs 2,780 crore in cash from buyers in the same quarter.

Revenue is different. DLF follows what is called the completed contract method. Under it, revenue is counted only once a project is finished and an occupation certificate arrives. That certificate is the official paper that says the building is ready for people to live in.

So a home booked years ago shows up as revenue only when its tower is done. DLF's CFO Badal Bagri said the revenue from the Rs 75,000 crore of launched projects will be recognised over the next four to five years, with the turning point in 2027 to 2028.

Why the three numbers look so different

In the same three months, DLF had three very different numbers. Bookings show how much buyers promised. Collections show how much cash came in. Revenue shows only what was handed over and finished.

Its managing director Ashok Tyagi named three "growth engines": strong pre-sales, strong cash and margins, and a growing rental business from offices and malls, according to Mint. He said revenue would grow a lot as homes launched after Covid are completed.

Is the selling going well?

Mixed. The Rs 3,800 crore of bookings was lower than the Rs 4,332 crore booked in the same months last year. The company said fewer new homes came to market.

For the first half of the year, April to September, DLF booked homes worth Rs 4,457 crore. Its target for the full year 2026-27 is around Rs 20,000 crore. That means it needs about Rs 15,500 crore more in the next six months. It is like a batting side that has scored slowly in the first innings and is counting on big hitters at the end.

Those big hitters are new launches. DLF plans the next phase of its Mumbai project, The Westpark, in the October to December quarter. Its luxury retirement project in Gurugram, The Aureva, sold all of its 172 homes, and prices at its super-luxury project The Dahlias went up 10 per cent this quarter.

A bigger plot of land in Gurugram

DLF also said it signed a collaboration for a fresh 7.48 acres on Golf Course Extension Road in Gurugram. It sits right next to about 28 acres the company took over around two years ago. Together, they will make one 36-acre parcel in Sector 61.

In a "collaboration", a landowner and a builder team up to develop land, instead of the builder buying it outright. DLF made a small payment for the new piece, and Tyagi expects to finish the whole deal by the end of March. The company did not share the total land cost or a launch date, though its presentation points to a launch in FY28.

Golf Course Extension Road has become a busy area for luxury homes. Oberoi Realty, Godrej Properties and Sobha have also announced projects there, as per The Economic Times.

Where is the cash?

Revenue may arrive late, but cash is already flowing. DLF said its operating cash flow was "yet another quarter of sustained cash generation", and its net cash, the cash left after paying off debt, stood at Rs 15,084 crore.

The company also estimates its launched projects could produce a surplus of about Rs 42,460 crore over several years. That is roughly Rs 27,500 crore from homes already sold plus roughly Rs 15,000 crore from homes still unsold. Think of it as a samosa stall that has taken orders for the whole week: the money is coming, it just arrives one plate at a time.

Any bumps on the road?

Yes. Tyagi said construction spending could dip for a while as workers travel home for the festive season and as pollution rules under GRAP, the Graded Response Action Plan, limit building work in the National Capital Region. He said contractors and labour plans are in place, and that things should ease once the restrictions are lifted.

The big lesson

When a builder says "sales", it usually means bookings. When it says "revenue", it means finished homes handed over. The gap between the two can be years long. DLF's own numbers show both sides: plenty of homes sold, and a big wave of revenue it expects from FY28 onward.
